title: The Federalist Paper Analysis
text:
For this project, I decided to complete option A and conduct a hypothesis test simulation study. I will simulate behavior under the null hypothesis analyzing average sentence length of the main authors of the Federalist Papers (Alexander Hamilton and James Madison), which were 85 essays written between 1787-1788 under the pseudonym Publius. As a (former) politics major these papers are important to me, because I had to read all of them in Intro to American Government. For those who are not politics majors, the Federalist Papers were critical to public acceptance of the U.S. Constitution, leading to its eventual ratification. They were written to explain the Constitution and its benefits to the populace. *Note: Although there were three authors, because John Jay only wrote 5 essays he has been excluded from this study.
I am investigating sentence length because it is one indication of writing style, as some people tend to write more “matter-of-fact” and to the point, while others may write “long, beautiful prose”. For those that do not have the time or energy to read the Federalist Papers in their entirety (increasingly common in our 2026 society), I have constructed this analysis to determine the writing style of the authors. For those inspired, I hope this analysis may spark an interest in reading the actual texts.



I will measure the length of sentences by counting words per sentence through a permutation simulation.
Step 1: calculate average sentence length of each essay.
Step 2: compare the average sentence length per essay between Hamilton and Madison.
I will conduct a 2-sided permutation test with a significance level of 0.05 (industry standard in psychology research methods, which I am currently taking)





“Did the main authors of the Federalist Papers, Hamilton and Madison, write sentences of notably different average lengths?”





Null Hypothesis (H0): Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of the same average length in their papers.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of different average lengths in their papers.




I’ve loaded the data from a public GitHub upload by Nicholas Horton.

report_words_clean <- readr::read_csv('https://github.com/nicholasjhorton/FederalistPapers.git')







Show Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(FederalistPapers)

data("FederalistPapers")

# view datasets in package
data(package = "FederalistPapers")

title: The Federalist Paper Analysis
text:
Final Summary:
For this project, I analyzed the writing patterns for Hamilton’s and Madison’s essays that make up the Federalist Papers. To do this, I cleaned the original data (uploaded by Nicholas Horton), evaluated average sentence length per paper and per author, ran the simulation 5,000 times under the null hypothesis, using the simulation function and mapping, visualizing my findings through a boxplot and histogram. I also calculated the observed difference and p-value for my simulation to determine if there was statistically significant evidence to reject the null (p < 0.05), which turned out to be 0.86 (much larger than 0.05). This indicates there was not a significant difference between the sentence length of both authors.

title: The Speeches of Hamlet
text:
This is a full text analysis project using dialogue from Shakespeare’s play Hamlet. I analyze character strings to answer the following research questions: 1. Who is the biggest yapper (i.e. who talks the most) in Hamlet? 2. How does language about love compare to language about death?




Cleaning data code
library(randomcoloR)
library(tidyverse)
library(forcats)
library(stringr)
library(plotly)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

hamlet <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/hamlet.csv')

hamlet <- hamlet |>
  filter(
    !str_detect(
      character,
      regex("stage direction", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(dialogue), !is.na(character)) |>
  mutate(
    character = str_remove_all(str_trim(character), ":\\s*$")
  )







Creating the yapper database
# Count words in each phrase.
hamlet_words <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    word_count = str_count(
      dialogue,
      "\\b[[:alpha:]]+\\b"
    )
  )

# Add words per character, per act. 
act_words <- hamlet_words |>
  group_by(act, character) |>
  summarise(
    total_words = sum(word_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )






Creating the yapper visualization
# making the color differences between characters more visible
character_levels <- act_words |>
  group_by(character) |>
  summarise(total = sum(total_words), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total)) |>
  pull(character)

set.seed(102)
character_colors <- randomcoloR::distinctColorPalette(
  length(character_levels)
)

names(character_colors) <- character_levels

act_plot <- ggplot(
  act_words,
  aes(
    x = act,
    y = total_words,
    fill = fct_reorder(character, -total_words, .fun = sum),
    text = paste0(
      "Act: ", act,
      "<br>Character: ", character,
      "<br>Words: ", total_words
    )
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = character_colors
  ) + 
  labs(
    title = "Who Speaks the Most in Each Act of Hamlet?",
    x = "Act",
    y = "Total Words Spoken",
    fill = "Character"
  ) +
  theme_gray()

ggplotly(act_plot, tooltip = "text")









For Question 1, I used an interactive, plotly stacked bar graph to visualize the characters that speak the most (Hamlet) and the least (Guildenstern). Each bar represents one of the 5 acts in the play. The colors represent each character, and if you click on a character’s name in the key the plot will isolate only their data.
From the bar graphs, you can see that the top 5 biggest yappers are all male characters (Hamlet, King Claudius, Lord Polonius, Horatio, and Laertes), followed by Ophelia in 6th place. What does it say about the focus of this piece that so many lines are spoken by the same 5 men?






Does this play care more about love or revenge (through death)?
love_pattern <- "\\b(love|loves|loved|loving|lover|lovers)\\b"

death_pattern <- "\\b(death|dead|die|dies|died|dying|kill|kills|killed|killing)\\b"

love_death <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    love_count = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      love_pattern
    ),
    death_count = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      death_pattern
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(act) |>
  summarise(
    Love = sum(love_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    Death = sum(death_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Love, Death),
    names_to = "Theme",
    values_to = "Occurrences"
  )






Show Code
love_you_pattern <-"\\blove\\b(?=\\s+you\\b)"

love_you_count <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    love_you = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      love_you_pattern
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(character) |>
  summarise(
    total_love_you_pattern = sum(love_you, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(total_love_you_pattern > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(total_love_you_pattern))

love_you_count

1 Hamlet                         1

behind_love_pattern <- "\\w+(?= love[sdr]?)"

behind_love_words <- hamlet |>
  filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(dialogue), behind_love_pattern)) |>
  mutate(word = str_extract(str_to_lower(dialogue), behind_love_pattern)) |>
  select(word, everything())

#complete bar chart
behind_love_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  #dont use slice_max(frequency, n = 15) |>
  head(15) |>
ggplot(
  aes(
    #x = frequency,
    x = reorder(word, n)
  )) +
  geom_bar(fill = "purple", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "15 Most Common Words Appearing Before 'Love' in Hamlet",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"), 
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 15, 20)
  ) + 
  coord_flip()














Line chart code
love_death_plot <- ggplot(
  love_death,
  aes(
    x = act,
    y = Occurrences,
    color = Theme,
    group = Theme,
    text = paste0(
      "Act: ", act,
      "<br>Theme: ", Theme,
      "<br>Occurrences: ", Occurrences
    )
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Love vs. Death in Hamlet",
    x = "Act",
    y = "Number of Word Occurrences",
    color = "Theme"
  ) +
  theme_gray()

ggplotly(love_death_plot, tooltip = "text")








Summary table code
act_totals <- love_death |>
  group_by(act, Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = sum(Occurrences),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Theme,
    values_from = Total_Occurrences,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  act_totals,
  caption = "Love and Death Word Occurrences by Act"
)

  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = sum(Occurrences),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  overall_totals,
  caption = "Total Love and Death Word Occurrences in Hamlet"

This analysis compares the frequency of love and death related words across Hamlet’s 5 acts. It counts related terms using word patterns using an interactive plotly line chart.
Act 1 contains an equal amount of love and death (15 occurrences each). However, the theme of love quickly rises throughout Acts II and III. In Act II, the theme of death is at its lowest, but it peaks around the climax of the play in Act IV. Themes of love peak in Act III, right before Ophelia’s death.
I think its interesting how the theme of love peaks and then drops right before the same happens with the theme of death. I wonder if this could indicate the central focus of the story on violence/death > romance, seeing how taking action/revenge in the face of corruption is central to the climax of the piece, while Hamlet’s romance with Ophelia serves to build up to this turning point.

title: The Speeches of Hamlet
text:
Conclusion
While I didn’t go into this project with gender in mind, I found that my data inadvertently highlights disparities between the amount of speech male versus female characters have (see Plot 1). Additionally, the fact that there are 10 more occurrences of death than there are of love indicates a greater focus on the theme of death in the play Hamlet.
